title: My Life With the Chimpanzees · teacher study guide

sections.title: Reread the memoir
teach: A memoir tells about real events in the writer’s life. Read Goodall’s whole memoir first so you understand what happened.
On your second reading, ask: What problems did she face? What did she learn? How did her work change over time?
When a question names a paragraph, reread that paragraph and the sentences around it. Use a detail from that part to explain your answer.
sections.where: Readings → My Life With the Chimpanzees → PDF pages 1–10 (textbook pp101–110). The memoir has paragraphs 1–61.

example.prompt: How can rereading help you answer a question about Goodall’s work?
example.thinking: I look for the part that answers the question. If the question asks about her early problems, I reread the beginning instead of choosing any detail about a chimp.
example.answer: I would reread paragraphs8–13 to learn about her early problems. The chimps ran away, so she had to change how she watched them.
example.why: The answer tells where to look and explains why that part is useful.

sections.tryPrompt: Where would you reread to learn what her research became?
sections.tryAnswer: Reread paragraphs60–61 on PDF page10. They describe the later research and the center.

sections.title: Find the main idea
teach: The topic is what a text is about. This memoir is about Jane Goodall’s work with chimpanzees. The main idea tells the most important point about that topic.
Goodall keeps trying, watches carefully, gains the chimps’ trust, and makes discoveries. Help from other people also supports her work.
A good main idea fits the whole memoir. Check it against the beginning, middle, and ending. One exciting event is a detail, not the main idea of the whole text.
sections.where: Readings → PDF page2, paragraphs8–10; page3, paragraphs11–17; page6, paragraphs38–39; page10, paragraphs60–61.

example.prompt: What is the main idea of this memoir?
example.thinking: I think about the whole story. I connect her early problems with her later discoveries and the research center.
example.answer: Patient, careful work can lead to important discoveries. At first, the chimps ran away from Goodall. She kept trying and changed her approach. Later, she made discoveries and helped build a research center.
example.why: It gives one main idea and supports it with details from different parts of the memoir.

sections.tryPrompt: Why is “The memoir is about chimps” not a full main idea?
sections.tryAnswer: That names the topic. A main idea must also tell an important point, such as how patient, careful work led to discoveries.

sections.title: Learn the six vocabulary words
teach: Read the sentence around an unfamiliar word. Try a meaning, put it into the sentence, and check whether it makes sense.
Vanished means disappeared. “The deer vanished into the bushes” means the deer could no longer be seen.
Miserable means very unhappy or uncomfortable. “The cold rain made the wait miserable” shows discomfort.
Irritable means easily annoyed. An irritable person may get upset over a small interruption.
Threateningly means in a way that warns of possible harm. A dog that growls threateningly may be warning someone to stay back.
Impetuous means acting quickly without thinking enough. Cutting fabric before measuring it can be an impetuous choice.
Dominate means to control or have power over. Someone who interrupts everyone may try to dominate a discussion.
sections.where: Readings → PDF page2: vanished; page7: miserable, irritable, threateningly; page8: impetuous; page9: dominate. Read the whole sentence around each margin word.

example.prompt: Use “impetuous” in a sentence that shows its meaning.
example.thinking: I need to show a quick choice made without enough thought. The action should help the reader understand the word.
example.answer: I made an impetuous choice when I cut the fabric before checking the pattern, and the sleeve turned out too short.
example.why: The sentence shows both the rushed choice and its result.

sections.tryPrompt: How are irritable and threateningly different?
sections.tryAnswer: Irritable means easily annoyed. Threateningly describes a warning of possible harm. Being annoyed does not always mean threatening someone.

sections.title: Use the comma rules
teach: A subject tells who or what a clause is about. A verb tells an action or a state of being. A clause has a subject and a verb. An independent clause is a complete thought: “Maya kept notes.” A dependent clause needs more to finish its meaning: “Although the camera failed.”
Use a comma before and, but, or so when the word joins two complete thoughts: “The camera failed, but Maya kept notes.” Each side can stand alone.
Do not add a comma just because you see and. “Maya checked the camera and changed the battery” has one subject doing two actions.
Use a comma after a dependent clause at the beginning: “Although the camera failed, Maya kept notes.” The comma goes where the opening clause ends.
Use a comma after a long opening phrase: “After several hours beside the marsh, Maya packed her notebook.” This opening is a phrase because it does not have its own subject and verb.
Use a comma after an opening transition: “For example, Maya recorded the time.” Other examples are “In fact,” and “After all,”.
Use commas in a list of three or more things: “She packed paper, pencils, and binoculars.” In these questions, include the comma before the final and. This is called a serial comma.
sections.where: Use the teacher’s comma rules in the study guide. For sentence examples in the memoir, open Readings and inspect complete sentences; the examples below are original teaching examples.

example.prompt: Why does this sentence need a comma? “Although the clay cracked, I repaired the sculpture.”
example.thinking: I find the two parts. “Although the clay cracked” needs another clause. “I repaired the sculpture” is a complete thought.
example.answer: The comma comes after the opening dependent clause, “Although the clay cracked.” It separates that opening from the complete thought, “I repaired the sculpture.”
example.why: It names both parts and explains why the comma belongs between them.

sections.tryPrompt: Add the comma and explain it: “The costume tore but Maya repaired it.”
sections.tryAnswer: The costume tore, but Maya repaired it. Both sides of but are complete thoughts, so the comma goes before but.

sections.title: Explain the author’s purpose
teach: The author’s purpose is the reason the author wrote the text. Ask: What does Goodall want readers to learn or understand?
Goodall informs readers about her research and what she learned about chimps. She tells about her own experiences and explains why the discoveries mattered.
Her feelings make the memoir interesting, but entertainment is not her only purpose. Her observations also teach readers about chimpanzees.
sections.where: Readings → PDF page6, paragraphs38–39; page10, paragraphs60–61. Compare what happened with the explanation of why it mattered.

example.prompt: Why did Goodall write about the tool discovery?
example.thinking: I explain what the event teaches readers. I do more than name the topic or say that the event was exciting.
example.answer: Goodall wants readers to understand an important discovery about chimps. She describes David changing a twig into a tool and explains why this challenged an old belief about humans.
example.why: It states a purpose and uses a detail to explain that purpose.

sections.tryPrompt: Why is “to entertain readers” only part of Goodall’s purpose?
sections.tryAnswer: The events can be interesting, but Goodall also teaches readers about her research and discoveries.

sections.title: Explain what she learned about chimps
teach: Goodall learned that chimps use tools and can change materials to make tools. David stripped leaves from a twig before using it to get termites.
She learned that chimps are individuals. They have different personalities, and their family relationships affect how they act.
She also saw young chimps learning from others. Chimps use calls and gestures to share information. Some gestures look like human gestures, but their calls are not the same as human language.
When you explain a discovery, tell what she saw and what it helped her understand. Do not make a bigger claim than the detail supports.
sections.where: Readings → PDF page6, paragraphs38–39 (tools); page8, paragraphs48–54 (individuals and family); page9, paragraphs55–56 (learning, calls and gestures).

example.prompt: What did Goodall learn about chimp communication?
example.thinking: I reread paragraph56. Then I explain what the calls and gestures show without claiming that chimps speak just like humans.
example.answer: Goodall learned that chimps share information through calls and gestures. In paragraph56, she describes signals that help chimps know what is happening. Some gestures look like ours, but their calls do not form a language in the same way human words do.
example.why: It explains a discovery, points to a paragraph, and keeps the claim accurate.

sections.tryPrompt: What is the difference between using a tool and making a tool?
sections.tryAnswer: Using a tool means using an object to do a job. Making a tool means changing material so it can do the job, as David did when he removed leaves from a twig.

sections.title: Describe Jane’s personality and success
teach: A personality trait describes how a person usually thinks or acts. Choose a trait, name an action from the text, and explain how the action shows that trait.
Goodall is persistent: she keeps trying after setbacks. She is patient: she gives the chimps time to get used to her. She is careful: she writes down details from her observations.
Her success came from these choices and from help from other people. Success does not mean she was never afraid or that she did everything alone.
sections.where: Readings → PDF pages2–3, paragraphs8–17 (setbacks and adjusted observation); page7, paragraphs45–46 (reflection and records); page10, paragraph61 (collaboration and research center).

example.prompt: How does Goodall’s note-taking show a personality trait?
example.thinking: I choose an action first. Then I explain which trait that action shows.
example.answer: Goodall is careful. In paragraph46, she adds details to her notes while the events are still fresh in her mind. This helps her save useful information for later research.
example.why: It names a trait, gives a detail, and explains how the detail supports the trait.

sections.tryPrompt: How do her early problems help show persistence?
sections.tryAnswer: The chimps kept running away, but Goodall continued trying and changed how she watched them. Keeping at a difficult task shows persistence.

sections.title: Explain why this text is a memoir
teach: A memoir is nonfiction about real experiences from the writer’s own life. The writer looks back and explains what those experiences meant.
Goodall took part in the events she describes. She uses first-person words such as I and my, tells what happened, and shares her thoughts and feelings.
The word I alone does not prove that a text is a memoir. A made-up story can use I, too. A memoir tells real personal experiences and reflects on them.
A memoir usually focuses on a meaningful part of a person’s life. An autobiography usually covers more of the person’s life.
sections.where: Readings → PDF page1, paragraphs1–4 (time, place and participant); page3, paragraph17 (looking back); page10, paragraphs60–61 (later meaning and result).

example.prompt: Why is My Life With the Chimpanzees a memoir?
example.thinking: I check that the events are real, that Goodall took part in them, and that she looks back on what she learned.
example.answer: This text is a memoir because Goodall tells about her own real experiences studying chimps. She describes what she did and how she felt. She also looks back on what she learned and how her research grew.
example.why: It explains several memoir features instead of only pointing to the word I.

sections.tryPrompt: Does every story that uses I count as a memoir? Why or why not?
sections.tryAnswer: No. Fiction can use I. A memoir tells about real experiences from the writer’s life and looks back on what they meant.
